exercise.answer: The operating system starts the .NET host, the host selects a runtime, and the CLR loads OrderFlow's assemblies and executes their managed IL. The CLR supplies services including JIT compilation, garbage collection, exception handling, type safety, and threading.

exercise.answer: After `dotnet build`, the project DLL under `bin/<configuration>/<target-framework>` contains Common Intermediate Language and metadata, not C# source or fixed machine code. The CLR can then JIT that IL for the current runtime and processor.

exercise.task: Explain when a method becomes native code and why the generated code can depend on the current machine and runtime.
exercise.expected: The async flow completes without blocking and ends with the Stage 03 pass marker.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: A method is normally JIT-compiled when it is first needed. The JIT can use the active processor features, operating environment, runtime version, and observed tiering information, so the resulting native code can differ between machines and can be re-optimised later.

exercise.task: Choose one allocation and one exception in OrderFlow and name the CLR service managing it.
exercise.expected: The async flow completes without blocking and ends with the Stage 03 pass marker.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: Creating an `Order` allocates a managed object whose reachable lifetime is tracked by the CLR garbage collector. Throwing an `InvalidOperationException` enters the CLR's managed exception-unwinding path. “Managed” means these runtime services govern execution; it does not mean the application never calls native code.

exercise.task: Identify two short-lived OrderFlow allocations and explain why GC frees reachability-based memory but does not replace `using` for external resources.
exercise.expected: The async flow completes without blocking and ends with the Stage 03 pass marker.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: Short-lived request DTOs and temporary LINQ result objects are typical OrderFlow allocations. The GC reclaims managed objects that are no longer reachable, usually cheaply in generation 0. It cannot deterministically release an external handle such as a file, stream, or database connection, so those resources still need `using`/`Dispose` (or `await using`).

exercise.task: Copy an `int`, then copy an `Order` reference in scratch code; mutate the referenced object and explain the different results.
exercise.expected: The async flow completes without blocking and ends with the Stage 03 pass marker.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: Copying an `int quantity` copies its value, so changing the copy does not change the original. Copying an `Order` variable copies a reference; both variables can observe mutations to the same order object. The distinction is value semantics versus object identity—not the oversimplification “stack versus heap.”

exercise.task: Locate the host setup and endpoint mapping, then explain how ASP.NET Core turns OrderFlow into a long-running HTTP service.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Use the focused concept only; do not copy unrelated lines. The answer must visibly demonstrate `WebApplication.CreateBuilder`, `MapControllers`, `Run` before you compare it with the reveal.
exercise.answer: It is a cross-platform framework built around a host, dependency injection, configuration, logging, middleware, routing and endpoint frameworks such as controllers or minimal APIs.

exercise.task: Trace one `POST /api/orders` request from socket to response and write the stages in their actual order.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: For `POST /api/orders`: Kestrel accepts the connection, middleware runs in configured order, routing selects the endpoint, model binding and validation create the request DTO, the controller calls application/domain logic, EF Core persists through SQLite, and result execution serialises the response as HTTP.

exercise.task: Find every service registration and middleware call, then label each as setup-time or request-time work.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Use the focused concept only; do not copy unrelated lines. The answer must visibly demonstrate `AddScoped<IOrderService`, `UseAuthentication`, `MapControllers` before you compare it with the reveal.
exercise.answer: `builder.Services` configures the DI container. After `builder.Build()`, `app.Use...` composes middleware and `app.Map...` adds endpoints before `app.Run()` starts the host.

exercise.task: Identify which process listens for HTTP, what reverse proxy would sit in front in production, and what application code runs after acceptance.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: The OrderFlow API process hosts Kestrel, which listens for HTTP. In production, a reverse proxy or load balancer may terminate public traffic before forwarding to Kestrel. After acceptance, ASP.NET Core middleware and the selected endpoint execute application code.

exercise.task: Move through the middleware calls in order and predict what would break if authorization ran before authentication.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Use the focused concept only; do not copy unrelated lines. The answer must visibly demonstrate `UseAuthentication`, `UseAuthorization`, `MapControllers` before you compare it with the reveal.
exercise.answer: A middleware delegate receives `HttpContext` and `next`. Code before `await next()` runs inbound; code after runs outbound. Order determines correctness for routing, auth, errors and caching.

exercise.task: Follow one controller action from bound request DTO to application service result; circle any business rule that should not live in the controller.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Use the focused concept only; do not copy unrelated lines. The answer must visibly demonstrate `[ApiController]`, `IOrderService`, `NotFound()` before you compare it with the reveal.
exercise.answer: With `[ApiController]`, routing attributes, binding conventions and automatic validation responses support API endpoints. Controllers should coordinate; domain rules belong in services/domain code.

exercise.task: Write the final URL for `Get(Guid id)` and explain how the `{id:guid}` constraint changes matching.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Use the focused concept only; do not copy unrelated lines. The answer must visibly demonstrate `[Route("api/orders")]`, `[HttpGet("{id:guid}")]` before you compare it with the reveal.
exercise.answer: Endpoint routing combines templates, route values, constraints and metadata. Attribute routes such as `api/orders/{id:int}` make contracts explicit.

exercise.task: Match list, create, and pay operations to GET, POST, and PUT, then justify idempotency expectations for each.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: OrderFlow uses GET for reading orders because it is safe and idempotent, POST for creating an order because creation is not inherently idempotent, and PUT for setting `/api/orders/{id}/pay` because repeating the same target state should be idempotent.

exercise.task: For successful create, missing order, invalid input, unauthenticated, and forbidden requests, predict the status code before running tests.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: A successful creation returns 201 Created; an unknown order returns 404; invalid input returns 400; a missing or invalid identity returns 401; and an authenticated caller without the required permission returns 403. The test should predict these before asserting them.

exercise.task: Compare `CreateOrderRequest`, `CreateOrderCommand`, and the domain `Order`; list one reason each boundary has a different shape.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Use the focused concept only; do not copy unrelated lines. The answer must visibly demonstrate `CreateOrderRequest`, `CreateOrderCommand` before you compare it with the reveal.
exercise.answer: Request and response DTOs control fields, validation and versioning. Mapping prevents callers from over-posting internal properties and decouples the external contract from persistence.

exercise.task: Send one valid and one malformed JSON body and identify which values bind before the controller action runs.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: A valid JSON body is parsed by the input formatter and bound to the action's request DTO before the action runs. Malformed JSON cannot be parsed and produces a 400 response under `[ApiController]`; validation can also reject a successfully bound but invalid model before business logic executes.

exercise.task: Break one data-annotation rule, send the request, and inspect the automatic validation response without adding the invalid object to the domain.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Use the focused concept only; do not copy unrelated lines. The answer must visibly demonstrate `[Required`, `[Range(1, 10_000)]` before you compare it with the reveal.
exercise.answer: Data annotations or custom validators produce model-state errors; `[ApiController]` can automatically return a structured 400 response. Domain invariants still belong deeper.

exercise.task: Create a development JWT, call the protected endpoint without it, with the wrong role, and with `OrderManager`; record 401, 403, and success.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: Create a development token with `dotnet user-jwts`. No valid token should produce 401; a valid identity without `OrderManager` should produce 403; a token with that role should reach the protected action. Authentication establishes identity, then authorization evaluates policy.

exercise.task: Locate the EF repository and DbContext, then draw the mapping from Order aggregate to SQLite tables.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: OrderFlow registers a scoped `OrderDbContext` with SQLite and maps `IOrderRepository` to `EfOrderRepository`. The aggregate is configured in `OnModelCreating`, migrations reproduce the schema, and repository LINQ is translated to SQL at materialisation.

exercise.task: Trace one repository query from LINQ expression to SQL execution and back to domain objects.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: The repository starts with `db.Orders`, composes `Include`, filtering, or projection as an `IQueryable`, and executes SQL at an async terminal operator such as `SingleOrDefaultAsync`. EF then materialises the returned rows as mapped domain objects.

exercise.task: Find the DbContext registration and explain why one scoped instance represents one web-request unit of work.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: `AddDbContext<OrderDbContext>` registers the context as scoped by default. One request can therefore share one identity map and save boundary, while unrelated concurrent requests get different non-thread-safe context instances.

exercise.task: Identify the aggregate root exposed as `DbSet<Order>` and why `OrderLine` is reached through the aggregate instead.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Use the focused concept only; do not copy unrelated lines. The answer must visibly demonstrate `DbSet<Order>`, `Set<Order>()` before you compare it with the reveal.
exercise.answer: It exposes query composition and state-changing methods such as `Add` and `Remove`; the actual database call usually happens on enumeration or `SaveChanges`.

exercise.task: Read the repository query and mark which operators become SQL and where materialisation occurs.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: Operators before `ToListAsync` remain in the EF expression tree and supported operations become SQL. `ToListAsync(cancellationToken)` is the materialisation boundary; filtering added afterward runs in memory rather than in the database.

exercise.task: Change a consumer to accept `IEnumerable<Order>` and prove it needs enumeration, not mutation or indexed lookup.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: A consumer that only filters and enumerates orders can accept `IEnumerable<Order>`; it does not need mutation methods or indexed access. EF's `IQueryable<Order>` carries an expression tree for SQL translation, but after materialisation the consumer should work with the in-memory sequence contract it actually needs.

exercise.task: Find the read-only list query, keep `AsNoTracking`, and explain why the pay workflow must load tracked state.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: The read-only list query keeps `AsNoTracking` because no entity changes will be saved, reducing tracking overhead. The pay workflow loads a tracked order so EF Core can detect the state change and write it during `SaveChangesAsync`.

exercise.task: Trace the state change before and after `SaveChangesAsync`; identify the point at which database persistence can fail.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: The domain object changes first, EF tracks that state, and `SaveChangesAsync(cancellationToken)` sends database commands. Persistence can fail at that await because of constraints, concurrency, connectivity, cancellation, or transaction failure, so the HTTP boundary must not report success before it completes.

exercise.task: List migrations, check for pending model changes, and connect one migration operation to the current model.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: `dotnet ef migrations list` shows known migrations, `has-pending-model-changes` checks model drift, and `database update` applies pending operations to SQLite. Review generated operations/SQL before production because migrations can lock, lose, or transform data.

exercise.task: Inspect the order-line loading strategy and explain how an accidental per-order query would change the query count.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: Loading orders and their required lines in one shaped query (or a bounded split query) keeps query count predictable. Querying lines inside a loop changes one list query into 1 + N round trips—one initial order query plus one extra query for every returned order.

exercise.task: Trace the interface from controller dependency to implementation registration and confirm the API project does not construct the service directly.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Use the focused concept only; do not copy unrelated lines. The answer must visibly demonstrate `interface IOrderService`, `ListAsync`, `MarkPaidAsync` before you compare it with the reveal.
exercise.answer: The interface describes application operations and lets infrastructure or presentation depend inward on a stable contract. It is also a natural transaction and authorisation orchestration boundary.

lessons.title: 88. Controller Should Not Become the Whole Application

exercise.task: Take one rule or mapping from a hypothetical fat controller and place it in the application or domain layer, then justify the boundary.
exercise.expected: The solution builds cleanly. When the API is running, the exercised request follows the status and response path described here.
exercise.hint: Use the focused concept only; do not copy unrelated lines. The answer must visibly demonstrate `CreateOrderCommand`, `orderService.CreateAsync`, `CreatedAtAction` before you compare it with the reveal.
exercise.answer: Thin controllers keep HTTP binding/status concerns at the edge while application services own use-case orchestration and domain objects own invariants.

exercise.task: Replace a concrete dependency in your mental model with its interface and identify the test seam this creates.
exercise.expected: All unit and integration tests pass, and you can name which boundary the selected test controls.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: `OrderService` depends on `IOrderRepository`, not an EF repository constructor call. The DI container supplies the runtime implementation, and a test can supply an in-memory fake. That visible constructor seam reduces coupling and makes the service independently testable.

exercise.task: For each OrderFlow registration, name the service, implementation, and lifetime; then resolve which layer owns the registration.
exercise.expected: All unit and integration tests pass, and you can name which boundary the selected test controls.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: Read each registration as service contract → implementation → lifetime. Domain/application code owns the abstraction, Infrastructure owns the adapter, and the API composition root chooses the mapping. Registration happens during startup; resolution constructs the graph when a request needs it.

exercise.task: Classify DbContext/repository, TimeProvider, and stateless receipt sender as scoped, singleton, or transient, and explain captive-dependency risk.
exercise.expected: All unit and integration tests pass, and you can name which boundary the selected test controls.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: `DbContext` and its repository are scoped so one request shares one unit of work. `TimeProvider.System` can be singleton because it is shared and thread-safe. A stateless sender can be transient unless its underlying client is deliberately shared. A singleton must not capture a scoped dependency, or request state can escape its scope.

exercise.task: Trace who constructs `OrderService` at runtime and contrast that with the service constructing its own repository.
exercise.expected: All unit and integration tests pass, and you can name which boundary the selected test controls.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: At runtime the ASP.NET Core container constructs `OrderService` and passes its registered repository and sender. If `OrderService` called `new EfOrderRepository(...)`, it would control construction and depend on infrastructure. DI inverts that control so composition stays at the application boundary.

exercise.task: Assign validation, domain state, persistence, HTTP mapping, and receipt delivery to their current classes; flag any class with two reasons to change.
exercise.expected: Your design names the problem being solved, the new failure mode introduced, and the metric that would validate the decision.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: Order owns domain state and invariants; validators check request shape; the repository persists; the controller maps HTTP; and the receipt sender handles delivery. A controller that also prices orders or sends receipts has multiple reasons to change and should delegate those responsibilities.

exercise.task: Add a hypothetical receipt implementation without editing `OrderService`; explain which abstraction makes that extension possible.
exercise.expected: Your design names the problem being solved, the new failure mode introduced, and the metric that would validate the decision.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: A new `SmsReceiptSender` can implement `IReceiptSender` and be selected in DI without editing `OrderService`. The abstraction creates a deliberate extension point: service behaviour is open to a new adapter while the use case remains closed to modification.

exercise.task: State the promises an `IOrderRepository` implementation must keep so an in-memory or EF version can substitute safely.
exercise.expected: Your design names the problem being solved, the new failure mode introduced, and the metric that would validate the decision.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: Both in-memory and EF implementations must preserve the repository contract: accept the same valid IDs and cancellation behaviour, return equivalent found/not-found results, persist according to the stated semantics, and surface failures consistently. A substitute that silently changes those promises violates LSP even if it implements the interface.

exercise.task: Check whether any OrderFlow consumer is forced to depend on repository operations it never uses; propose a split only if it improves a real consumer.
exercise.expected: Your design names the problem being solved, the new failure mode introduced, and the metric that would validate the decision.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: Inspect consumers before splitting. A read-only query handler should not depend on save/delete operations if those members create real coupling; a command handler may need a write contract. Keep one cohesive repository if every consumer genuinely uses the same small capability set—ISP does not require an interface per method.

exercise.task: Draw the dependency arrows and verify Domain/Application do not import Infrastructure or API.
exercise.expected: Your design names the problem being solved, the new failure mode introduced, and the metric that would validate the decision.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: The dependency arrows point API → Application → Domain, while Infrastructure implements interfaces consumed inward. Domain and Application do not import API, EF Core, or SQLite. At runtime DI supplies the outer implementation without reversing the compile-time dependency direction.

exercise.task: Apply The Core Idea to the current OrderFlow architecture. Name the problem it solves, the trade-off it introduces, and the signal that would justify it.
exercise.expected: Your design names the problem being solved, the new failure mode introduced, and the metric that would validate the decision.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: Inward dependencies keep OrderFlow's business policy independent of HTTP and SQLite, making core rules easier to test and adapters replaceable. The trade-off is extra projects, interfaces, and mapping. Introduce the boundary when business rules or external integrations have enough independent change to justify it.

exercise.task: Apply Example Project Layout to the current OrderFlow architecture. Name the problem it solves, the trade-off it introduces, and the signal that would justify it.
exercise.expected: Your design names the problem being solved, the new failure mode introduced, and the metric that would validate the decision.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: Domain holds order rules; Application holds use cases and ports; Infrastructure implements EF/SQLite and delivery adapters; API owns HTTP and composition. This separates change boundaries but adds navigation and mapping. It is justified when the solution has meaningful business logic and replaceable external concerns.

exercise.task: Apply Why Do This? to the current OrderFlow architecture. Name the problem it solves, the trade-off it introduces, and the signal that would justify it.
exercise.expected: Your design names the problem being solved, the new failure mode introduced, and the metric that would validate the decision.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: Clean boundaries stop framework and persistence details spreading into business rules, improving testability and replaceability. They cost indirection, mapping, and more concepts. Use them when longevity, team size, domain complexity, or integration volatility makes that cost worthwhile—not simply because a diagram looks tidy.

exercise.task: Run one domain test, deliberately break the protected rule, observe the failure, then restore it.
exercise.expected: All unit and integration tests pass, and you can name which boundary the selected test controls.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: Run the named domain test: its production collaborator set is only the domain object and in-memory values. Breaking the invariant should make the assertion fail; restoring the rule should pass it again. That red-then-green observation proves the test protects behaviour rather than merely executing code.

exercise.task: Use the small repository and receipt fakes to control one service outcome; state the interaction you care about instead of mocking every call.
exercise.expected: All unit and integration tests pass, and you can name which boundary the selected test controls.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: Use the repository fake to return a controlled order and the receipt fake to record delivery. Assert the meaningful outcome—for example, one receipt after a successful payment—rather than every internal call. A fake supplies working behaviour; a mock is only needed when the interaction itself is the requirement.

exercise.task: Run the API integration tests and identify which components are real, which are replaced, and why SQLite is used.
exercise.expected: All unit and integration tests pass, and you can name which boundary the selected test controls.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: The integration test uses the real ASP.NET Core pipeline, routing, model binding, DI, EF Core mapping, and SQLite provider. External identity/time or outbound delivery may be replaced for determinism. SQLite exercises relational behaviour more faithfully than EF's non-relational in-memory provider, though it still does not prove production-provider parity.

exercise.task: Describe the external E2E journey—from HTTP client through database—and list what the current in-process integration test does not prove.
exercise.expected: All unit and integration tests pass, and you can name which boundary the selected test controls.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
exercise.answer: A true E2E journey starts outside the deployed process, sends HTTP through its real network/reverse-proxy boundary, authenticates, writes the configured database, and observes the public response and side effects. The in-process integration host does not prove packaging, deployment configuration, TLS/proxy behaviour, or the real external services.

exercise.task: Define one realistic create-order load scenario, target latency/error thresholds, and the environment data needed before running it.
exercise.expected: All unit and integration tests pass, and you can name which boundary the selected test controls.
exercise.hint: Start from the current OrderFlow checkpoint. Say the input, boundary or failure you are examining before choosing a code or design change.
